title: Case Studies Published in Students' Journal
outcomes: Analyse strategy in R&D-led regulated industries.
Apply Ind AS 38 to research and development spending.
Evaluate international expansion and transfer pricing.
Apply CSR rules and ethical leadership principles.

meta.exam_tip: Separate research from development by the feasibility date before computing any capitalised amount.

concepts.title: Strategy in regulated, R&D-led industries
body: Pharmaceutical, agrochemical and similar firms compete through R&D pipelines, patents, regulatory approvals and manufacturing quality. Strategy choices include innovator versus generic, contract manufacturing, in-licensing, and expansion into regulated or emerging markets.

Porter's five forces explain profitability: buyer power (hospitals, governments), supplier power (API makers), threat of substitutes (generics after patent expiry), entry barriers (approvals, capital) and rivalry. Value chain analysis shows where cost or differentiation is created — R&D, quality, distribution.
Leaders balance short-term profit with long-term investment, and must align growth with compliance, pricing regulation and patient safety.
concepts.analogy: Patents and approvals are the moat.
concepts.work: Patent expiry invites generics and erodes margins quickly.

concepts.title: Accounting for research, development and intangibles
body: Under Ind AS 38, research expenditure is expensed. Development cost is capitalised only when the entity can show technical feasibility, intention to complete, ability to use or sell, probable future economic benefits, adequate resources, and reliable measurement of expenditure.

Acquired patents and licences are recognised at cost; intangibles with finite lives are amortised, those with indefinite lives are tested for impairment annually under Ind AS 36. Internally generated brands and customer lists are never capitalised.
Auditors focus on capitalisation judgements and impairment of development assets, often reporting them as key audit matters under SA 701 for listed companies.
concepts.analogy: Research is expense; development may be an asset.
concepts.work: Clinical trial costs before feasibility is shown are expensed.

concepts.title: International expansion and transfer pricing
body: Entering markets such as Africa raises questions of entry mode (export, distributor, subsidiary, joint venture), regulatory registration, currency and payment risk, and FEMA rules on overseas investment.

Transactions with associated enterprises abroad are international transactions; income is computed using the arm's length price determined under section 165 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 by the most appropriate method — CUP, resale price, cost plus, profit split, TNMM or another prescribed method.
Under-pricing exports to a subsidiary shifts profit abroad and invites adjustment; documentation and benchmarking protect the company. Treasury hedges currency exposure on receivables.
concepts.analogy: Price group transactions as if between strangers.
concepts.work: Charging a subsidiary less than unrelated buyers leads to an upward adjustment in India.

concepts.title: CSR, sustainability and ethical leadership
body: Section 135 applies to a company with net worth of ₹500 crore or more, turnover of ₹1,000 crore or more, or net profit of ₹5 crore or more in the preceding year. It must spend at least 2% of average net profits of the three preceding years on Schedule VII activities through its CSR policy.

An unspent amount linked to an ongoing project goes to an Unspent CSR Account within 30 days of year-end and is spent within three years; other unspent amounts go to a Schedule VII fund within six months of year-end.

Large listed companies report ESG performance through the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report. Ethical leadership covers fair pricing of essential medicines, transparent clinical data and protecting whistle-blowers.
concepts.analogy: Doing good is also a compliance duty.
concepts.work: A company with ₹1,450 crore turnover must comply even if profits dip.

illustrations.title: CSR obligation of Calyx Pharma
illustrations.q: Calyx Pharmaceuticals Ltd. had net profits (computed under section 198) of ₹84 crore, ₹96 crore and ₹120 crore in the three preceding years and a turnover of ₹1,450 crore last year. It spent ₹1.4 crore on CSR this year, all on a hospital project that will run for two more years. Compute the CSR obligation and explain the treatment of the shortfall.

illustrations.q: Calyx sells 10,000 kg of an active pharmaceutical ingredient to its wholly owned subsidiary in Kenya at ₹1,000 per kg. Comparable sales of the same ingredient by Calyx to unrelated buyers in similar markets and terms are at ₹1,200 per kg. Determine the arm's length adjustment and the method.

summary: Five forces and patents shape pharma strategy.
Ind AS 38: research expensed; development on six criteria.
Transfer pricing: ALP under section 165, Income-tax Act 2025.
CSR: ₹500 crore NW / ₹1,000 crore turnover / ₹5 crore profit; 2% of average.
Unspent: 30 days to Unspent CSR Account, or 6 months to fund.
remember: Internally generated brands are never capitalised.
traps: Using current year profit for CSR.

viva.q: Can internally generated brands be capitalised?
viva.model: Ind AS 38 prohibits recognising internally generated brands, so they stay off the balance sheet.

viva.q: Why do auditors flag development cost capitalisation?
viva.model: Because it involves significant judgement on feasibility and future benefits, making it a key audit matter.

viva.q: What entry modes are available for a new foreign market?
viva.model: Exporting, distributors, licensing, joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries.
The Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report through which large listed companies disclose ESG performance.

viva.q: What happens to unspent CSR money not linked to an ongoing project?
viva.model: It is transferred to a Schedule VII fund within six months of year-end.

cases.title: Calyx Pharmaceuticals — integrated case
cases.case: Calyx Pharmaceuticals Ltd., a listed company, spent ₹60 crore this year on a new diabetes molecule: ₹22 crore on early laboratory research and ₹38 crore on late-stage development after the molecule cleared feasibility tests, with funds committed to finish it. Its key patent on a blockbuster drug expires next year. Calyx also sells to its Kenyan subsidiary below prices charged to unrelated distributors.
